description:
Astro Vitals is a passionate and innovative student team from Benchmark Junior School, GT Road Campus, Islamabad, Pakistan, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

Our team is driven by curiosity, creativity, and a shared passion for science, technology, space exploration, and innovation. Through our project, Astro Vitals – Health Monitoring System, we aim to explore innovative ways of combining healthcare technology with space science to address health-monitoring challenges.
summary:
Our team, Astro Vitals 6, developed a Smart Health Monitoring System to help astronauts monitor important health measurements during space missions.

Our project combines hardware, software, and Artificial Intelligence (AI). The hardware includes an ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30105 sensor, OLED display, and rechargeable battery. The MAX30105 uses optical sensing technology to monitor heart rate (BPM), estimate blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and detect changes in blood flow. It also provides red, infrared, and green light readings for further analysis. Temperature, blood pressure, and ECG monitoring require additional sensors.

The ESP32 processes sensor data and displays readings on the OLED screen. We also developed a connected website where users can view their health results. Our AI-powered assistant helps astronauts understand health information, identify possible concerns, and explore potential solutions.

Our project addresses the need for accessible health monitoring in space, where immediate medical assistance may not always be available. It provides a portable way to access important health information and helps astronauts stay aware of changes in their bodies.

Our goal is to contribute to safer space missions through affordable technology, real-time monitoring, connected software, and AI-assisted support. By combining these features, we hope to improve astronaut well-being and support future space exploration.
details:
Project Details – Astro Vitals 6

Smart Health Monitoring System

Our team, Astro Vitals 6, developed a Smart Health Monitoring System to support astronauts in monitoring important health measurements during space missions. Our project combines hardware, software, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to provide accessible health information through one connected system.

How Does It Work?

Our device uses a MAX30105 optical sensor to monitor heart rate (BPM), estimate blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and detect changes in blood flow. An ESP32 microcontroller processes the sensor readings and displays them on an OLED screen. The device is powered by a rechargeable battery, making it portable. We also developed a web-based dashboard where users can view their health results. Additionally, our AI-powered assistant helps astronauts understand health-related information and explore possible solutions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The system provides a convenient way to monitor important health measurements and helps astronauts stay aware of changes in their bodies. Since immediate medical assistance may not always be available in space, accessible health information can support better-informed decisions. Our goal is to contribute to astronaut well-being and safer space exploration.

Tools and Technologies

  • Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30105 sensor, OLED display, rechargeable battery.
  • Hardware Programming: Bare-metal C using the Arduino IDE.
  • Dashboard Development: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • AI: AI-powered assistant for health-related guidance and information.

Creativity and Innovation

Our creativity lies in combining a portable health-monitoring device, an interactive website, and AI assistance into one connected system. Rather than displaying sensor readings alone, we aim to make health information easier to understand and more useful.

Factors Considered

Our team considered portability, affordability, battery life, ease of use, accessibility, and the challenging environment of space. We also considered measurement reliability and clear presentation of health information. Our project is a prototype, and further testing and additional sensors would be required before it could be used for medical monitoring in actual space missions.
